pr_title: Auto populate primary key column for updatable database views
pr_body:
Fixes #49950.

Some databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB) support updatable `VIEW`s. Why not get the primary key's value automatically (via `RETURNING`, for the databases that support it) when inserting a record? This PR addresses this problem.
pr_comments: What is needed to move forward with this PR? It's kind of a bummer that there is a major regression in a new version of Rails and it takes us so long to fix it. It would be great if this fix can be included in the next 7.1.x release so other people don't have issues with PostgreSQL views.

There are some legit CI failures, at least the ones for composite primary key models. I think I have an idea how to simplify the fix to avoid dealing with composite primary key issues while fixing the reported problem
https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/49950#issuecomment-1895881930
@nvasilevski should this PR be closed? Feel free to close.

Yes, thank you for your work!
Substituted by https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/50783

issue_context.title: The object does not have an `id` if it is an instance of a Rails model in which the table is a Postgres view.
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce
The object does not have an `id` if it is an instance of a Rails model in which the table is a Postgres view.

This worked in Rails v7.0.8 and fails in v7.1.1.
<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->
```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  git_source(:github) { |repo| "https://github.com/#{repo}.git" }

  # Activate the gem you are reporting the issue against.
  gem "activerecord", "~> 7.1.0"
  gem "pg", "~> 1.5.4"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(ENV.fetch("DATABASE_URL", "postgres:///"))
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query(<<~SQL)
  create temporary table animals (
    id int primary key generated by default as identity,
    name text not null
  );
SQL

ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query(<<~SQL)
  create temporary view dogs as SELECT animals.id, animals.name FROM animals;
SQL

class Dog < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.primary_key = :id
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_id_is_returned
    dog = Dog.create!(name: "Jack")
    assert(dog.id)
  end
end

```

### Expected behavior
`dog.id` should have the value from the database.

### Actual behavior
`dog.id` is `nil`

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 7.1.1

**Ruby version**: 3.2.2
comments: Thanks for the report. I think I know what the problem is. Will try to come up with a PR.

I was thinking about the issue and about the fix we are considering and wanted to dig a little bit further. It looks like at least in postgresql views won't have any indication of any auto-populated column, not just the primary key. For example if we tweak the schema a little bit:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query(<<~SQL)
  create temporary table animals (
    id int primary key generated by default as identity,
    name text not null,
    purchase_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
  );
SQL

ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query(<<~SQL)
  create temporary view dogs as SELECT animals.id, animals.name, animals.purchase_date FROM animals;
SQL
```
The same assertion will fail for the `purchase_date`:
```ruby
    dog = Dog.create!(name: "Jack")
    assert(dog.purchase_date)
```

Basically because `Dog._returning_columns_for_insert` is an empty list.

So I think to simplify the fix we need to approach it in the following way:
Currently: We want to always append `primary_key` to `_returning_columns_for_insert` list
Possible new approach: Append `primary_key` to `_returning_columns_for_insert` only if the original `_returning_columns_for_insert` is empty, meaning that Rails wasn't able to find any value that needs to be auto-populated which means we should fallback to the previous behavior of returning PK.
I believe this should simplify the fix as currently it's a little tricky with composite primary key models and mysql not allowing to return anything other than a single value.


Ultimately I think we should try to make sure every autopopulated column from the view is returned but for now we can focus on PK to at least preserve the previous behavior.

@fatkodima let me know what you think and if you'd like to try this approach out. Also let me know if you prefer me doing it. I don't mind, just didn't want to take over this work since you've already come up with a possible fix. Thanks
@nvasilevski Yes, please try that approach, if you will. Do not currently have time to investigate it further.

Should be fixed by https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/50783 and backported to `7-1-stable`
Please feel free to reopen if the fix doesn't work or it didn't cover your corner case. Thank you!

The fix does not solve my problem and the test in the code example informs that id does not exist.
ruby 3.2.2
rails 7.1.0
I can't reopen this issue, should I create a new one?

review_comments:
MySQL, as always, "surprises" by its behaviour. 

Rails uses `SHOW FULL FILEDS` to get the table's schema info. This works for views too. But, for regular tables for primary keys it returns something like
```
mysql> SHOW FULL FIELDS FROM books;
+------------------------+--------------+--------------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+---------------------------------+---------+
| Field                  | Type         | Collation          | Null | Key | Default | Extra          | Privileges                      | Comment |
+------------------------+--------------+--------------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+---------------------------------+---------+
| id                     | int(11)      | NULL               | NO   | PRI | NULL    | auto_increment | select,insert,update,references |         |
``` 

but for views it returns something like this
```
mysql> SHOW FULL FIELDS FROM printed_books;
+--------+--------------+--------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+---------------------------------+---------+
| Field  | Type         | Collation          | Null | Key | Default | Extra | Privileges                      | Comment |
+--------+--------------+--------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+---------------------------------+---------+
| id     | int(11)      | NULL               | NO   |     | 0       |       | select,insert,update,references |         |
```

(note the that the default is set to 0 😱)

So we need to remove this check, because it will always be set to 0. Not sure why it was added initially, seems like redundant.

Ok, CI fails, turns out that this is needed, because MySQL does not support `RETURNING`.

MySQL databases have autoincrement keys starting from 1, but it is possible to configure them to start from 0. How is it safe to assume that real-world applications never do this? With this assumption I can make this code work for MariaDB.
This is a great find, we end up merging https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/50783 which fixes views for postgresql but keeps mysql views broken so we still need to look into it

Unless I'm missing some corner-case `columns` array should always include primary key column which means the condition will be true at least for one column in the list.
I think instead of making the check we should always push the `primary_key` value to the list and make sure the resulting list is unique

I was reading https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/50001 issue and I think it made me realize that always appending `primary_key` may not be correct, especially if the key is composite. 
Because in case of MySQL we still can only get one value back which is `last_inserted_id` and we won't know which part of the composite primary key to assign it.

However maybe we could start from always appending a single-column PK to the list.
@nvasilevski I'd say it's good enough to special case for a single-column PK?
